To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have identified the chemical formulas of the molecules produced upon interaction of ionization radiation with simple methane ices.

we have identified for the first times the presence of alkanes, alkynes, alkenes and alkadienes in methane ices exposed to ionizing radiation, and that these products have molecular weights of up to 300 amu.

we present a novel approach to the analysis of complex organic molecules formed upon interaction with ionizing radiation, and we provide evidence of the formation of high molecular weight hydrocarbons in the form of alkanes, alkynes/dienes and alkenes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the chemical makeup of complex organic molecules synthesized in astrophysically relevant ices.
the chemical evolution of interstellar ices and the origin of complex hydrocarbon molecules, which are of astrobiological interest as they are precursors to life.
the chemical evolution of interstellar and cometary ices.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the chemical complexity observed for methane ices exposed to ionization radiation in the laboratory is consistent with the chemical complexity of ices observed on Pluto and other outer Solar System objects, which have been irradiated over their lifetime by energetic particles and photons.

our results show the potential of the reflectron time-of- flight mass spectrometer in combination with a soft photoionization source to analyze ices and to provide molecular formulas of the newly synthesized molecules.
methane ices exposed to ionizing radiation produce a wide variety of hydrocarbons.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

our results show the potential of reflectron time of flight mass spectrometry in combination with soft photoionization for the identification and quantification of complex molecules in astrophysically relevant ices.
our results are in agreement with the chemical composition of the Pluto-Charon system as observed by the New Horizons spacecraft.
our data provide evidence for the formation of high-molecular weight alkanes, and that the formation of these molecules is enhanced in the case of deuterated methane.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the chemical composition of the ices on the surface of Pluto and the Kuiper Belt objects is much more complex than previously thought.
the chemical complexity of radiation processed ices is not only limited to the formation of amines but includes a broad spectrum of high-molecularweight hydrocarbons.
reflectron time-of flight mass spectrometry, coupled to photoionization, is an excellent technique for probing complex organic mixtures.
